paragraphs.source_en: The bathhouse is such a jumble that I truly do not know where to begin. These monsters do nothing by any rule, so it is quite a labor to explain them in proper order. Let me begin with the tub. Whether it really deserves to be called a tub is hard to say, but let us call it one. It is three feet wide and nine feet long, divided in two, with one side filled with milky-white bathwater. This, they say, is a medicinal bath, clouded white as though lime had been stirred into it. Nor is it merely cloudy in color; it is greasy and utterly opaque. On inquiring closely, I learned there was no wonder it looked rotten, for they change the water only once a week. The pool in the other half is said to contain ordinary bathwater, but I swear it, too, can by no means be called clear or sparkling. Judging from its color, the most exact comparison would be rainwater in a fire cistern after it has been stirred up. Now comes the account of the monsters. Ah! This is truly hard work to describe. In the bath like a fire cistern stood two young fellows, standing there and splashing water noisily over their bellies; they certainly knew how to amuse themselves. In the contest of dark complexions, neither of them yielded an inch to the other. I thought to myself: these two monsters are fairly robust. Presently one of them, rubbing the front of his chest with a towel, said to the other, “Kin, this place always hurts somehow. What do you suppose it is?” Kin earnestly advised him, “That is your stomach. The stomach is a thing that can take your life; if you are not careful, it is dangerous.” The man pointed to the region of his left lung and said, “But it is on the left.” Kin replied, “Then it is certainly the stomach. The stomach is on the left and the lungs are on the right.” “Is that so? I had always thought this was where the stomach was.” So saying, he tapped his waist this time. Kin said, “That is a hernia.”

paragraphs.source_en: Just then a young man of twenty-five or twenty-six, with a slight moustache, plunged in with a splash, and at once the soap suds and grime from his whole body floated up to the surface. The water immediately took on a layer of bluish-gray, glittering oily scum. On the surface beside him two heads were visible, and one bald old man addressed a young man with close-cropped hair: “When one gets old, one is no good anymore. Once a man's head and feet stop working properly, he cannot compete with the young fellows. Still, when it comes to bathwater, if it is not hot, even now I feel it lacks something.” The young man said, “Sir, you are sturdy enough. It is fine to have as much vigor as you do.” “I have no vigor! It is only that I have not fallen ill. So long as a man does not do foolish things, he can live to one hundred and twenty.” “Well! Can a person live that long?” “He can! I will guarantee one hundred and twenty! Before the Restoration, in Ushigome, there was a direct retainer named Magaribuchi, and a servant in his house lived to be one hundred and thirty.” “That is a remarkably long life.” “Yes, yes; he lived so long that at last he forgot his own age. They say he remembered his age up to one hundred, but after that he forgot it. When I knew him he was exactly one hundred and thirty, but he had not died then, and what became of him afterward I do not know. For all I know, he may still be alive now.” Saying this, the old man stepped out of the tub. The young man with the slight moustache was scattering soap suds like flakes of mica all around himself and grinning to himself.

paragraphs.source_zh: 就在这时，一个二十五六岁、长点小胡子的青年咚地跳了进来，这一下不打紧，他满身的肥皂沫和身上的污垢立刻飘到水面上来。水也就立刻浮上一层带青灰色的、闪闪发光的油垢。在他旁边的水面上露出两个脑袋，其中一个光脑袋的老头儿向一个留有寸头的青年搭话说：“老了，不中用啦。人要是头、脚都不灵了，就比不过小伙子啦。不过，唯独对于洗澡水，如果不热，我还是觉得不够味。”那小伙子说：“老大爷，您够结实的啦。有您这样精神也就满好啦。”“精神不济啦！只不过是还没有病罢了。人只要是不干荒唐的事儿，可以活到一百二十岁呢。”“嘿！能活那么久呀？”“能活！一百二十岁没问题！在维新前牛込区有个叫曲渊的直参武士，他家的一个仆役就活了一百三十岁。”“那可活得真长啊。”“是哟，是哟，因为活得太长啦，连自己的岁数都记不起来了。据说他在一百岁以前，还记得自己的岁数，以后就记不住了。我认识他的时候正好他是一百三十岁，可那时他还没有死，以后怎样我就不知道了。说不定现在还活着呢。”说着，这老头儿跨出了浴池。刚才那个留有小胡子的青年，把他身旁的水弄得飘满了云母片一样的肥皂沫，独自嘻嘻地笑着。
